newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Slim majority see Fed rate hike July 1-2.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Slim majority see Fed rate hike July 1-2.

text.p: A resilient U.S. economy, bolstered by robust consumer spending and low unemployment, will probably prompt the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates this summer, said economists polled by Reuters.

A slim majority of the experts said the Fed would boost the Federal funds rate 25 basis points at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 1-2. More than three-fourths of those surveyed saw a rate hike by the end of August.

Twenty of 37 economists surveyed on Friday and Monday said they expected the central bank to lift the Federal funds rate to 5.75 percent from its current 5.50 percent level at the July meeting. Thirty of the 37 pundits said the Fed would lift that key target rate at least 25 basis points before or at the FOMC meeting on August 19.
The central bank left interest rates unchanged May 20. It raised the Fed funds rate by 25 basis points on March 25.
Analysts said a tight labor market and strong consumer demand were the Fed's main concerns even though current inflation readings have been tepid.
The economists contended that the Fed's role in monetary policy is to fend off possible future inflation.
"The (May) employment report (due on Friday) looks to be pretty healthy," said Joseph Dziwura, vice president and an economist at the Sakura Bank, Ltd.
"We think the Fed is running out of patience with the unemployment rate," said Dziwura, who forecast an unemployment rate of 5.0 percent for May.
The U.S. Labor Department said the 4.9 percent jobless rate in April matched the rate in December 1973 and was the lowest since a 4.8 percent rate in November 1973.
Other analysts cited consumer sentiment as the driving force behind the U.S. economy's vibrant expansion.
Consumer demand is showing the most strength, said David Blitzer, vice president and chief economist at rating agency Standard & Poor's.
"Consumer spending in the first quarter was strong, even with the slight reduction in (Friday's) Gross Domestic Product number (GDP)," said Blitzer.
The second reading of first-quarter GDP rose by 5.8 percent, a tad lower than the 6.0-percent rise Wall Street experts had expected.
Blitzer said the average consumer is starting to see price increases in various sectors, such as services, entertainment related goods and movie prices.
"We are beginning to see prices creep up in a lot of places ... and see somewhat few sales goods just because more goes to the full price," Blitzer added.
However, a few experts said the central bank would refrain from raising rates in the near future. They said that an eventual slowdown in consumer demand will be more pronounced than expected.

"The economy has begun to slow in the second quarter ... and we are not likely to see a bounce back in consumer demand in July," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
He said the manufacturing sector for the first time in this economic expansion appears to be retaining its strength even in the face of weakened demand.
"We've had a couple of months of slower demand and yet the emerging picture for manufacturing in May is that the manufacturing sector continues to grow," Kretzmer said.
Production could downshift if consumer demand turns sluggish while manufacturing and inventories continue to grow, thus hampering economic growth, he said.
A jump in the May National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index showed the manufacturing sector of the economy rebounded in May.
Kretzmer said he had anticipated a strong NAPM reading. He said the May retail sales number would indicate whether consumption is in a slowdown phase.
If not, Kretzmer said: "It's certainly possible the economy will bounce back and the Fed will end up making a move."
